text: We know what happens in these cases is that courts don't weigh the IQ evidence. They -- they don't say, well, the IQ  evidence is really strong for the state, let me weigh that against his inability to buy car  insurance or to maintain a bank account or something like that. They simply move on from IQ. And so, once you open the door to this kind of balancing test, the second prong is really malleable, really amorphous, and we're picking  up disparate facts about someone's life, self-reported or by biased reporters. And so that evidence is not disciplining the inquiry. It's not adding more rigor to figuring out what the intelligence is. And if it were, then the  IQ specialists would simply make a better IQ test that accounts for things like that.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: Okay. Thank you.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Justice Gorsuch?  Justice Kavanaugh?

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: So what are the different permissible Eighth Amendment  approaches a state can use when there are multiple scores?  For example, in your reply brief, you articulate the -- if the median is above 70. Is that  -- if the median's above 70, can the state say that's it?

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Robert M. Overing
text: Yes.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Okay. And you don't think Hall and Moore require more -- more analysis in those cases?  You think that's a safe harbor, so to speak?

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Robert M. Overing
text: Yes, states can adopt reasonably reliable methods. And the APA  handbook says that the median is option 1.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Okay. And if the  -- another approach you articulate is the overlap approach, the overlap among each scorer's error range. Same question there. If the overlap  --well, you're a little bit ambiguous about what the overlap needs to be to give you certainty. What  -- you want to explain that?  I know you think it's satisfied here, but what's the rule?

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Robert M. Overing
text: So the idea is that when there's a cluster of scores, that we can take into account each score's error range and then lay them on top of each other and see which numbers the error ranges have in common. So  the intuition there is that maybe his true IQ is somewhere in the middle.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: What if the bottom of the error  -- error range is 69 or 70, of the overlap error range?

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Robert M. Overing
text: I -- I don't think that's a problem for the state because the question is still the likelihood that his IQ is 70 or below. So simply having the number 69 in an error range, whether using the overlap or some other method, doesn't reflect a greater than 50 percent chance that his IQ is below 70.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: But, in any event, in this case, you say the bottom of the overlap is 73, I believe, correct?  At least that's what you say in the reply brief. You say 73 to 77.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Robert M. Overing
text: And I think that should be a 78, but that's on the most generous assumption about the error range being plus or minus five.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Okay. And is the composite score method another method that the  state can use, a state can use and, in your view, stop there?

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Robert M. Overing
text: Yes.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Okay.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Robert M. Overing
text: When it's available.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: And are there any other methods?

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Robert M. Overing
text: The average is a rough approximation of the composite score.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Well, there's a lot of skepticism about the average being accurate.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Robert M. Overing
text: Well, the author of the A  -- one of the authors of the APA's amicus brief in this case, Dr. Schneider, said that the average is a rough approximation of the composite score. Even if the composite score is the theoretically best method, states are allowed to adopt other methods. The fifth method would be to look at the high score when the highest score's entire error range is over 70. And those are the five that we've discussed as reasonably reliable methods.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: And why there -- this picks up on the Chief Justice's question. Why are you picking just the high score in that fifth approach?

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Robert M. Overing
text: The high score  --

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: That seems, as -- as he said, results-oriented.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Robert M. Overing
text: The  -- the high score is more probative because there are many ways that  an IQ score can err downward and very few ways that a score can err upward. And so especially to take into account the obvious incentive to malinger in these cases, the lowest score should be viewed with greater suspicion. Oklahoma has adopted a rule like this and it has withstood federal review for many years.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Then, to follow up on Justice Kagan's question, what's the logic or the rationale or the sense behind not having a district court or a trial court or a state court have the ability in those circumstances to go on and look at more?  Because I think what you were saying is each of those approaches are essentially a safe harbor. You win. The defendant can't  meet his or her burden in those circumstances, you win. The state court can't go on and look  at other things. That's, I think, what you're saying. What's the logic, the rationale, the sense behind that?

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Robert M. Overing
text: Well, the adaptive behavior prong is simply not as good as IQ, and so, once you start weighing that subjective and amorphous evidence against the objective evidence of IQ, we don't think it's within courts' capacities to do that well. Even if  clinicians could somehow weigh the evidence of the ability to buy groceries against the IQ score of 78, I don't know how courts would do that. Adaptive behavior was added later. Originally, the diagnosis was just based on IQ. There's great disagreement among the experts about what adaptive behavior even means. Is it  10 or 11 domains or three different domains? And there's great disagreement about how to even measure it. There are hundreds of different scales, inventories, batteries for adaptive behavior. I think people have a misconception that these are just other standardized tests, but often it's not, and there's a lot of judgment that goes into picking them. So I'll just give one example in this this case, a  -- a reading comprehension test. The courts below credited evidence that -- that  Mr. Smith is barely literate, I think at Petition Appendix 22, and then he was  administered a reading comprehension test that showed he reads at an 11th grade level, which is clearly inconsistent with intellectual disability, but the state courts focus on the  evidence from grade school. They pluck out a different fact. And so this is not a really rigorous scientific test the way that IQ is, the fruit of a multi-century enterprise to figure out the best possible estimate of intelligence.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Thank you.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Justice Barrett? Justice Jackson?

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: So I guess I'm trying to understand the basis for our being able to determine that the district court in this case erred, which is what I understand you to be asking us to do. So are -- are you saying that Alabama has selected any one of those five methods by legislation, for example, and the district  court refused to apply it in its consideration?

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Robert M. Overing
text: No, Alabama hasn't adopted one of those methods.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: All right. So you explored a number of possibilities with Justice Kavanaugh, none of which Alabama has actually  adopted, so we can't say that the district court erred by not applying Alabama law in that sense. Did you ask the district court to apply any of those methods in its consideration of  -- of this defendant's intellectual disability?

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Robert M. Overing
text: Well, it's the Petitioner's burden to come in --

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: No, no, no. Did  -- your  --your burden right now as Petitioner is to establish that the district court erred, and so what I'm trying to ask you is whether you're  saying that the district court erred by not evaluating this defendant in a way that he was  never asked to do by the state below.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Robert M. Overing
text: Well, it's a legal error because my answers to Justice Kavanaugh were that those are all reasonably reliable methods  that the state could adopt. And if that's true, then it doesn't matter whether Alabama  has, in fact, adopted them in statute because there's no Eighth Amendment violation.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: That was my first question. Doesn't it matter for the purpose of our evaluation of the district court's error  whether or not the district court was asked to evaluate this defendant using the method that you now say it was erroneous for the district court to not have used?

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Robert M. Overing
text: The  --

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: I mean, this never came up during -- like, no one said to the district court, please evaluate him using this method, and the district court said no. In that situation, we then assess whether the district court was wrong in refusing to adopt that method.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Robert M. Overing
text: We didn't get that far because we had five IQ scores that clearly show  he loses, and then the district court focused only on the 72. And so the question --

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: But the district court was weighing all of the evidence under  the standard that it seems like your expert also agreed was the right legal test at the time. And now you're saying the test should  have been different. The district court was only allowed to look at one of these other five reliable methods, although no one said to the district court at the time, please look at that method.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Robert M. Overing
text: We said to the district court Alabama law is a true IQ of 70 or below by a preponderance. And then the district  court did not apply that burden.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: Okay. Let me ask you this because I do think that there's something about party presentation here that's a little troublesome. A couple weeks ago, in a case called Clark versus Sweeney, we summarily reversed a grant of habeas because the court of appeals had granted habeas based on an argument that the petitioner had not presented -- had not presented. So I feel like you're actually asking us to violate that same principle. You never asked the court of appeals in this case, for  example, to evaluate the district court on the basis of these five methods and say that it was erroneous on that basis or on the cumulative -- on the cumulative effects test. I'm -- I'm a little confused all around because I thought the question presented in this case was about the cumulative effects test and that that's what you were actually advocating for. But that didn't come up in the lower courts. So how could we possibly reverse  on the basis of these kinds of arguments that were not presented below?

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Robert M. Overing
text: We absolutely did present evidence from Dr. King at JA 270 and 271 that his consistent scores were above 70. We didn't have to get to the level of granularity of specifying a particular method because there is no method in this case that can prove his IQ is likely 70 or below. We're offering those to answer the Court's question how to assess multiple IQ scores.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: And your  -- your answer is not  --

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Robert M. Overing
text: But it's sufficient to reverse.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: -- your answer is not something about cumulative effects is what the court had to do and didn't do?  I -- I thought that was the test that you were requiring us to consider as the thing that a district court has to do.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Robert M. Overing
text: Our first argument is that it didn't do that because it looked only at the possibility. And if the Court agrees  --

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: It didn't  -- wait.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Robert M. Overing
text: --it has to do that --

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: I'm sorry. I'm just  --I thought you were saying the district court erred because it didn't consider the cumulative effect of multiple IQ scores and  that the cumulative effect was a thing that the district court didn't do. All I'm asking here is, did you ask the district court to do that, or did you say to the court of appeals the district court has erred because it didn't look at the "cumulative effect" of the multiple IQ scores?

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Robert M. Overing
text: Yes, we said that in the district court. With Dr. King's testimony, we said it, and  --

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: Cumulative effect, I'll find it in the record?

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Robert M. Overing
text: We -- we  --we  --

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: Because I didn't see the words "cumulative effect" in the record.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Robert M. Overing
text: Well, there are lots of synonyms, but consistent scores above 70, that's the -- the same thing. And then, in the  Eleventh Circuit, we presented this evidence and said the district court didn't take seriously the whole of the IQ evidence because it didn't even mention his score of 78, so it couldn't have done the cumulative effect. That's enough to reverse. If the Court wants to go further and discuss the  reasonably reliable methods, we think that would be a good idea, especially for guidance for  --

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: So you're not asking necessarily for that rule about the reasonably  reliable methods?  That certainly did not come up before?

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Robert M. Overing
text: Well, that is the question presented, and so that would be a complete answer to Smith's claim, is that there  is no way that he can prove an IQ below 70 because, even on these common and expert -approved methods, he hasn't shown that his IQ is below 70.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: Thank you.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Thank you, counsel. Mr. Graver.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court:  Under Atkins, states have significant discretion in defining what it means to be intellectually disabled and what a defendant must do to prove it. Alabama has exercised that discretion to require that Respondent show  his true IQ is likely 70 or below based on all relevant evidence, including his multiple IQ scores all above 70. The courts below erred because they replaced that burden with some variant of a one-low-score rule. Everyone now agrees that such a rule is wrong. Instead, Respondent  focuses on justifying the opinions below as applying a holistic analysis. But that misses the point. The problem here is not that the courts below simply looked at other evidence. It is that they measured that evidence against the wrong standard, and it's that they looked at that evidence on only one side of the scale, never considering the collective weight of  Respondent's multiple IQ scores taken together. I welcome the Court's questions.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: THOMAS
text: What exactly did Atkins say the Eighth Amendment violation was?

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: I think Atkins laid down a general rule.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: THOMAS
text: Which  --which is?

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: Which is that you cannot execute the intellectually disabled, and the meaning of intellectual disability is something that states define with significant discretion.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: THOMAS
text: How did Atkins  -- what did Atkins say about determining what intellectual disability meant?  Actually, it  used the word "retardation."

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: Sure.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: THOMAS
text: What did it say that was?

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: I think that Atkins looked -- and the Chief Justice put this well in Moore  -- it's that the scope of Atkins reaches no further than the consensus of the states. So I think that to the extent there's content to that command, it's going to come from state consensus. But I really do think  that Atkins largely, much as this Court has done in the insanity context, outsourced the definition of "intellectual ability" to the states.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Counsel, I'd like to  -- you  --you're focusing in on Atkins, but Hall and Moore say something very different than what you're saying. In Hall, Mr. Hall had scores between -- nine scores over 40 years. The lower courts found a score of 71 and 80, only two of the scores, to be valid. But  Florida had a strict cutoff rule that said anyone with higher than a 70 could not be intellectually disabled. So you can't have a  flat rule that says you get one score over 70, you're not -- you're not disabled, correct?

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: Correct. I think that just  --yeah.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: And what Atkins also said, I'm quoting, "For professionals to  diagnose and for the law then to determine whether an intelligence disability exists once an SMN applies and the individual's IQ scores is 75 or below, the inquiry would consider factors indicating whether the person had deficits in adaptive functioning. Courts must  analyze the STEM, and if the STEM includes 70, the defendant must be able to present additional evidence of intellectual disability, including testimony regarding adaptive functions." So for us to say what Petitioner wants would disavow that language in Hall. It would  disavow nearly the identical language in Moore. In Moore, he had two valid scores of 74 and 78. Nowhere did we suggest that courts had to aggregate, cumulate, medium them out, composite them, do anything else with them. What we had -- and, there, the court held that  the state courts had violated Hall when it discounted the lower end of Moore's STEM because he was malingering. The tests were  valid. It had a SEM. The SEM was below 70. And then the Court held, once the SEM in some of those valid tests were below 70s, the courts "must continue the inquiry and consider other evidence of"  -- "of intellectual disability where an individual's IQ score adjusted for the test's standard error falls within the clinically established range for intellectually functioning deficits."  So you are asking us to tell courts below to do something substantially different  than what we told them to do in Hall and Moore.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: Respectfully, no, Justice Sotomayor. There's a big difference between saying you can move on and look at other evidence and saying you can then forget about IQ entirely.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Ah.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: The big problem here --

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Okay. That's something different. What you're talking about  then is not an  --a legal error by the courts below. You're talking about a different  -- your difference of opinion.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: No, it is a legal error twice over, and I think it's a helpful thing to spell out here, is that even if you look at other evidence, you still need to circle back  and see how that weighs against the evidence on the other side of the scale. And in this  context, that is going to be the multiple consistent IQ scores together.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Well, wait a  --

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: The two legal errors --

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: -- minute. But that's what the district  --that's what the two experts  -- the three experts here did. There was Dr. King, I think one was Dr. Chudy, who was the original expert, and then there was the evidentiary hearing, Dr. Fabian, if I'm not mistaken. Each one of them did exactly that. Your Dr. King looked at the scores and said, I'm looking at the functioning and I don't think he's on the lower end of 7 -- of 70 because, when I speak to him, he speaks well. He can respond. I think he functions at a higher rate. The other doctors, which the district court credited and did many, many more tests  than Dr. King did, looked at all of the tests, all of the results, and said I'm convinced that  his range is 70 and below.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: So, before turning to the experts, let me just emphasize what I think are two discrete legal errors with the way in which the courts thought about this under Alabama law. Even if you tend to look at the secondary evidence, you still need to circle back  --

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Are you saying it's wrong to do it?  Do you say Alabama says it's wrong to do that?

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: Wrong to do what?

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Look at secondary evidence.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: I don't think there's any per se rule in Alabama that says you cannot look at this. But the difference is --

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: So there's no per se  --

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Can you tell us what the two  --

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: Can you please tell us what the two legal errors are?

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: Sure.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Thank you.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: Thank you, Mr. Graver.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: So the basic idea is, where you have all of this evidence together,  are you measuring it against the right standard?  So one legal error that happened  below is that the courts swapped essentially a preponderance burden with a possibility burden. But the other part is, even putting that to the side, the difficulty is that you still need to figure out what the ultimate question Alabama law is asking here, which is, is this other evidence strong enough to drag down the collective weight of IQ --

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: So that seems --

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: -- below the line.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: -- totally right to me. So I'm  -- I'm wondering -- you -- you heard the question that I asked Mr. Overing, and I'm wondering if we disagree at all. If I say the thing that Hall and Moore require is that when you have a score that's 70 or below, you do have to give the defendant an opportunity to come in and to talk about adaptive functioning. But, having given the defendant the opportunity to talk about adaptive functioning,  yes, of course, you can go back to the scores and to the fact that there are a lot of scores on one side, the upper side of 70, that make you think that that evidence of adaptive functioning just cannot possibly carry the day. Is that what you're saying, or are you saying something more than that?

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: I think I agree with 95 percent or at least with one or two asterisks. And let me say how I think that cashed out here and then what the  constitutional rule is for how you just think about IQ. The issue is that what you were describing before just did not happen here. The only time that the courts grappled with --

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: Okay. So I  -- I take that point.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: Okay.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: Let's  -- let's presume that I don't care about it for the moment.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: Fair enough.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: You know, that all -- all I'm trying to do is to figure out the rule, and then we can go back and say whether the court did it or not do it.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: So I think that the part where I disagreed with what you said before is just in the sense that a single low score in all circumstances, no matter what, will always preclude a state from being able to focus on  IQ. So imagine, for instance, just a case --

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: No, I  -- I don't think it would  --it would  --the only thing that I think a  -- a single low score does is to say, yes, at that point, the defendant does have to have the opportunity to come in with adaptive evidence. And I take Hall and Moore to have -- that is their holding.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: Right. So I think I take it slightly less categorically than you do, which is just to say, so you imagine a case of, you know, 10 85s and one 72. The collective  error range of those scores, even if you look at the 95 percent confidence interval, is not going to grace 70 or below. So imagine a situation like that where -- you -- I think you can structure it where the possibility remains so low  --

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: Okay. So that's like the hypothetical that you gave in your brief,  like if there are a lot of 90s, and I kind of take that point, right, because, like, at some point, there's no clinician in the world who's going to say that just because you have, like, one outlier score, that -- that there's a possibility, right, if you have, like, six 90s and a 72. But, if you have something that's more along the lines of here  --

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: Mm-hmm.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: -- right, then I take it that we are in agreement, tell me if I'm not, that at that point, the Hall and Moore ruling is you have to allow the person to come in with adaptive functioning, evidence but, of course -- may I, Mr. Chief Justice?

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Sure.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: But, of course, you can say this is outweighed by the fact that  there's a multitude of scores on one side.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: Yeah, I think that there is broad  -- and if I can just stress the two key points of agreement is that moving on doesn't mean you're done. It involves circling  back to the standard that state law imposes. And I think, in turn with that, it's helpful to clarify what I think is now a point of agreement, that the one -low -score rule reading of Hall and Moore where prong 1 is  satisfied substantively so long as you have one low score is wrong.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: Right.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: Yeah.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: Okay.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Thank you, counsel. Justice Thomas? Justice Alito?

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: Let me see if I understand the colloquy you just had with Justice Kagan and  -- and the degree to which you agree with what she said. Did either Hall or Moore hold anything with respect to how a case must be treated when there are multiple scores?  Hall and Moore talk  about one score and they say that dealing with multiple scores is a complicated matter. But do they say anything about how a court is to deal with a situation where there are more than one scores?

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: No, not expressly.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: So, if there is a case with one score and the one -- the -- the standard error of measurement has a range that is below 70 and that's it, that's all that's in the case, one score, standard error of measurement is below 70, yes, they  --Hall says that allows the  -- the -- the -- the prisoner to proceed with evidence about adaptive functions, but it doesn't say how the Court is  to deal with a situation where there are multiple scores.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: That's correct. And this is what I was trying to get at before, is that I do think in a lot of the solutions that I think might come with concerns that come with looking at injecting adaptive functioning into  this space is I do think states have some discretion about when you want to sort of focus on IQ alone as a threshold matter. And I do think, to the extent that a defendant or  -- just can't come in and show that your multiple scores have any realistic possibility of dipping below any concerning  range, that is a time where a state can say we don't want to inject any of this other stuff  into it, just focus on IQ.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: Okay. So what we are looking for here under our precedents is the evolving standard of decency that exists on this issue about how to  -- how to decide whether a  --someone who's sentenced to death has significantly sub-average intellectual functioning. In prior cases where we have tried to determine what the national consensus is, we have looked at state laws, things that are enacted by the state legislature on the theory  that they reflect the moral judgment of the people of that state as expressed through their elected representatives. But what do we do with a situation -- and let's say that if state -- a state made the law through case law without being -- without thinking that it had to do something one way or the other because of our decisions about constitutional standards. Put that aside. What do we do with a situation like we have here, where state courts and lower federal courts are trying to figure out what we said in  --what Hall and Moore mean?  And so their decisions reflect their interpretations, perhaps erroneous interpretations, of those two precedents of this Court. Do we -- do we look at those to see whether there's a national consensus?

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: No, I don't think so. I think there's a difference between  -- the idea for a national consensus is when a certain moral judgment has the imprimatur of the  people. I don't think that happens when a court imposes that standard on an incorrect understanding of federal law. So, to the extent that this Court is still doing head -counting for purposes of Eighth Amendment, I don't think that courts misunderstanding Hall or Moore would factor in  favor for whatever new rule is being proposed.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: Now I don't know whether you've surveyed the state -- state  statutes, so perhaps you're not in a position to answer this question, but if one were to survey the state -- the statutes of -- of all the states that have the death penalty and see whether they have adopted one approach or  another approach to the situation we're dealing with here, what would we find?

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: So I don't -- I  --I can't speak to the legislatures just because I don't know what was motivating them. Alabama  was able to catalogue, I think, a few examples in their brief of instances where state courts were applying what is essentially the one-low- score rule. That erroneous understanding of Hall and Moore, which, again, we all agree is  an erroneous understanding of Hall and Moore, I don't think that that counts as a moral endorsement for the one-low-score rule.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: And Justice Kavanaugh asked your friend about the advantages and  disadvantages of a safe harbor as opposed to the alternative, and maybe you would -- I'd be interested in what you have to say about that. If there's a -- a safe harbor in the sense that a  -- a person sentenced to death who's claiming a intellectual disability has to  meet some concrete standard before the case can go on, will there not be greater consistency and predictability, and is that not one of the  -- the lodestars of the Court's death penalty jurisprudence, as opposed to a situation where everything is up for grabs in  -- in every case and both sides can bring in experts to testify about the person's intellectual disability or lack of intellectual disability and every trier of fact is going to decide that on an individualized basis?

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: So I a hundred percent agree with that, Justice Alito. And if I can  just emphasize one point because I don't think there's any practical daylight between what I'm saying and what Alabama was just talking about. I think just  -- the point I was making before is there might not be a per se legal bar in looking at the other evidence, but the IQ  evidence may nonetheless be practically dispositive in a given case. So what I'm understanding essentially what my friend was saying is, well, if we look  at the IQ scores, it was the Defendant, the Respondent's burden to essentially show at step 1 that the error range of those scores together  reaches 70 or below because, even if -- if that range never reaches 70 or below in the first  place, there's no realistic possibility that any of the secondary evidence on the other side of the scale is going to drag you over. So I think that that's just the  -- that's more of a practical matter with the facts of this case, where IQ happens to be dispositive just because there's not going to be anything on the other side of the scale that tips it over.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: Thank you.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: I'm not sure how that happens. There were nine scores in Hall  between 71 and 80, and we still sent it back for the court to consider additional evidence, including adaptive functioning, correct?  What Justice Alito was saying is states could do something like he suggests, but is that constitutionally required?

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: I think the difference, though, is --

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Answer my question. Would states have to do it that way?

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Or could they do it now in whatever way they thought, one of the five ways suggested by the other side or the way they're actually doing it now?

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: The answer is uncertain for the reasons I was explaining with Justice Kagan. And I can't  -- you know, I'm not good enough at math to do this on the fly, but the basic idea is that if those collective scores  do not produce a range that even grades at --

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Has any state adopted that measure?

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: --I don't think there's any constitutional bar --

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Has any state approached the issue that way with multiple scores?

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: I don't think so. I think our big  --

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Did Dr. King approach it that way below?

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: In part. I think he focused on IQ and said that it did not fall below 70 and then also said that the other evidence on the side  --on the other side of the ledger wasn't strong enough to show any other form of disability either.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: What I thought he did was exactly what all the experts did, is three of the five fell within intellectual  disability, and then he relied on adaptive functioning to say he thought he was not intellectually disabled.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: Let me make one quick point --

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Mm-hmm.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: -- just in addition to this, is that what you won't find in any of the expert reports is a conclusion with respect to what Alabama law asked. None of them found  that Respondent's true IQ was likely 70 or below. So finding that Respondent did not satisfy his state law burden  --

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: I'm sorry, who didn't find that?

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: No expert in this case  -- you won't find any  --

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Wait a minute. That's what they did say.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: No, no, it's  --it's a  --

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: That two of them  --at least two of Respondent's experts found he was intellectually disabled. That was  the finding the district court made.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: It depends what definition you're using. The experts were using clinical definitions that are distinct from Alabama law.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: I don't  --

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: No one made --

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: -- I don't --

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: Okay.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: -- disagree with you, but the district court was following Alabama law. It's  -- these things are not statutory. Most of these -- the very few, maybe Oklahoma is now, where one score above 76 disqualifies you. I don't know how that's not  different than the 70, one score above 70  situation might be, but we'll look at Oklahoma when it comes to us.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: Sure. The only thing I'll add is that I don't think the district court was following Alabama law because, as my friend emphasized, I think a very telling point is that you will not find a single sentence in anything the district court wrote that said Respondent's IQ is likely 70 or below. We think that they were laboring over  --

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Oh, is that what you think is  -- they did wrong?

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: I think that there's -- what I was trying to get at at the start is there's two problems. They misunderstood the  standard for a possibility idea from the one-low-score rule.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: That was only the Eleventh Circuit who said that. The district court certainly didn't say that.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: But then the basic part too is returning to what Alabama law is, which is a numerical inquiry, does the evidence show that you've been able to drag down the IQ scores below 70. There's no engagement with that. The basic I  --

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: But that  --that was never argued by Alabama.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: Oh, no, it -- it was one of their leading arguments, which was that you did not consider the totality of the evidence. And when you're trying to figure out whether  the secondary evidence drags --

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Counsel, that --

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: --the IQ down  --

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: -- that -- that's -- all right. I'll stop.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Justice  --

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: But that's attributing to one broad statement a specific argument that I don't see. Where did they say  that the adaptive functioning should be ignored because the cumulative effect of the scores showed he wasn't --

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: It's two sides of the same coin. What it's saying is there's no need  to move on to other stuff because, here, Respondent hasn't even carried his initial burden of showing it will do any good.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: All right. Thank you.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Thank you. Justice Kagan? Justice Gorsuch?

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: A few questions there where I don't think you got to finish your answer. Here's your shot.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: I would be pretending if I remember what any of those questions were. (Laughter.)

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: So, you know, I think, instead of, you know, turning myself in a circle, if there's anything, you know, that you wish I'd spoke to  --

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Well, no, no. Well, no, there isn't. I want to get what your argument is as I'm here to understand it.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: Right.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Not  -- not --not -- not anything else. And I think one of the questions was what do you think the error was that the district court made and that the Eleventh Circuit made?  I think that was one  question that I'd like to hear the answer to.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: Right. So I think there's two related errors. And the first is  what we were saying before, is that they just misunderstood what the substantive standard is. I'm going to look at this evidence, I'm going to ask whether there's a possibility. Alabama looks for a likelihood. So that's mistake number one. But the second part is, even if you say it's applying the right standard, there's still a basic analytical error because, once -- if you look at the opinions below, once the courts consider multiple IQ and conclude that it's theoretically possible Respondent's IQ dips to 70 or below, IQ falls out of the case entirely. And that's a basic analytical error  because, of course, not all possibilities are the same. A defendant with one score of 75 is going to have a really different burden than a  defendant with a hundred scores of 75. So the analysis here, what it should have looked like is taking account of that dynamic, which is not just saying, well, there's a possibility IQ falls away, I'm going to look at this secondary evidence. You then needed to circle back and  see if that secondary evidence was strong enough to drag down the IQ scores below the line set by Alabama law.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: And the first error, though, might be itself dispositive, it sounds like.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: Yeah, they're independent errors.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Either one of which is sufficient?

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: Correct.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Okay. And you agree that at the end of the day, before a federal court can grant habeas relief, it has to find a violation of the Eighth Amendment here?

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: Yes. Can I add one piece to it, is that  --

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: If you must. (Laughter.)

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: -- the --the wrinkle here which I think is a bit difficult is the innovation of Atkins  --

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Yeah.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: -- which is to --

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Innovation. That was the word I was looking for. (Laughter.)

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: -- which is to identify a federal rule, a general rule against executing the intellectually disabled but largely outsourcing its definition to state law.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: At -- at -- at bottom, though, I agree with that. That's an innovation for sure. But it was trying to give some breathing room to states.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: Mm-hmm.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: There has to be a floor, an Eighth Amendment floor, beneath all that breathing room, right?

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: Yes.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Presumably. And before a federal habeas court can grant relief, I would have thought you have to find a violation of federal law.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: Yeah, I think that  -- you know, make of it what you will, but I think the  -- the -- the formal way in which it would work is there's a violation of Atkins, federal,  because, one way or another, either met or did not meet or not even  --whether or not you satisfied Atkins turns on whether you satisfied state law.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Even if state law is well above the Eighth Amendment floor?

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: Oh, I understand. In that, I think that the answer would be probably yes, although I think it's difficult.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Really?  Is it that difficult?

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: Well, I think that states have broad discretion to set  --I do think that at some point  --what I will say -- you know, let me take that back just a little bit in that  --

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: I would think that you might want to.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: Yeah. That states are free to be more protective --

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Right.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: -- than what the Eighth Amendment requires.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: How many times have we held that, right?

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: A hundred percent. So, for instance, what I, you know, meant to say is imagine a state adopted the one-low-score rule as a matter of state law. Whether or not you violated that wouldn't necessarily implicate the Eighth Amendment because it's more protective than what the Eighth Amendment would require.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Exactly. And so  --

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: Yeah.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: -- before a federal habeas court could grant relief, it would still have to go beyond that and find a violation of the Eighth Amendment.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: Yes.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Okay. I would  -- I'm glad we got to that. Okay. And then what do you think about my  -- the -- the holding that I suggested to your friend from Alabama, you know, looking  at what Hall and Moore and trying to figure out, because I agree there is some confusion and that's why we took the case, the QP we did,  was trying to sort some of that out, that under Atkins, states can implement the first prong  however they want as long as they don't treat a single low score -- a single score in the low  70s as decisive, Hall, or use facts extraneous to IQ scores to outweigh a low score, Moore. Is that a correct and -- and fair summary of the law that would provide guidance, do you think?

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: A hundred percent.

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: On the  -- on the constitutional floor that you were just  exploring, I want to ask the questions to you that I was exploring with Alabama's counsel. If the median is above 70, I understood them to say that you  --the defendant cannot make out a successful Eighth  Amendment claim even if they might have something under state law. Do you agree with that?

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: I don't think that the Eighth Amendment necessarily speaks to that one way or another. I mean, again, I think --

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: So you don't agree with that then?

case_name: John Q. Hamm, Commissioner, Alabama Department Of Corrections, Petitioner, V. Joseph Clifton Smith, Respondent
speaker: Harry Graver
text: Well, I think that the standard for what the Eighth Amendment is at least under Atkins is going to only  -- the -- the Eighth Amendment strictures are only going to reach as far as a nationwide consensus mandates.
