case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Well  --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: THOMAS
text: Yeah.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: I'm sorry. Look, the -- what you're sketching out for us is a potential disaster. In other words, you're saying, if the candidate's going to win by 65 percent, no standing. But, if the  candidate, you know, hopes to win by a dozen votes -- and there are places in the country where that happens over and over again -- then  he has standing. But we're not going to know that until we get very close to the election, right?  And so it's going to be in the middle, the most fraught time for the Court to get involved in electoral politics. That's when you say we should jump in, as opposed to the more general, broad rule, Mr. Clement's broadest rule, I guess, is, look, he's a candidate. He's challenging a rule in the election. You know, isn't -- isn't that enough?  And one reason, as I say, we'll be deciding that case then, you know, six months, nine  months, maybe two years before the election, as opposed to the day after the votes have been counted.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: So I -- I -- I don't think that is an accurate description of our position for a couple of reasons. I don't think that there is a concern that standing will only be available right before an election and only in  close cases, and that's for two reasons. The first is that the evidence that a  -- a candidate plaintiff could use to show standing isn't simply sort of limited to  -- to polling data. I think Meese versus Keene is very helpful on this point. In Meese versus Keene, the Court described two types of information that the candidate used to establish standing. One was polling data. One was, you know, the expertise of a political advisor. But I don't even  think that those things are necessary in a case like this one, where we are dealing with a very experienced and successful candidate. Congressman Bost has been successfully running for election for 30 years. At the time  --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Well, I  --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: You know, when they  --when you run for election for 30 years and win, sometimes, you know, you get  --you -- you act as if you have no risk of losing. And you know what happens then?  You lose. A candidate who acts as if there's no risk of losing often  --often loses. I don't know -- and then you say rely on polling data. Are polls always reliable?

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: My point is simply that in response to the Chief Justice's question, I  think that there's a lot of information Congressman Bost could have brought to the  table. I don't think it's limited to polling data.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: But -- okay. I -- respectfully, bring the table, okay, so we bring to the table polling data that shows you're down 20. Candidates that are down 20 sometimes make late  -- late breaks for it and win. Happens all the time. And -- and -- and you said expertise of campaign advisors. I respect them as much as anyone, but they can be wrong and they don't have perfect crystal balls either. I don't understand a standing rule that therefore depends on prognostication, is my only point, and so you can respond to that as you think best.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: Yeah. Thank you, Your Honor. I -- I think that in -- in any standing case where a plaintiff is alleging future injury, courts are required to make some  sort of prediction. Now, but, of course, the prediction is a substantial risk of harm. It's not certainty of harm. And my point is merely that there is a lot of information that was available to Congressman Bost. He wouldn't even need to turn to the type of information that the Court credited in Meese versus Keene. He could have relied on, you know, the eight election cycles that he had participated  --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Well, there was a lot of  --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: You  --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: -- there was a lot of information  for, you know, Tom Dewey and Charles Evans Hughes, and, you know, they both went to bed thinking they were -- were President. And it just seems to me that the ability to predict has  -- is --is not -- has not been proven to be infallible. And yet you're going to tell somebody two weeks before the election, no, you -- you won last time by whatever margin. By the way,  what margin are you looking for?

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: Again --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Prior races he won by what and then that's enough to get standing?

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: So, again, this Court has not attached a metric. It uses the substantial risk test across the mine-run of standing cases. It has never attached a metric. What it has said is that you look -- you know, the burden is on the plaintiff and you look at the facts --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Yeah. No, that's --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: -- in the record, which is why I called the Court's attention to the declaration.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: No, that's right, but it depends on what sort of things you're talking about, the risk that the -- you know, the car is going to explode or whatever. But, if it's a risk of elections and all that counts is the -- the number you get, it does seem to me that it would fall upon the court to give some idea.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: Again, I do think that when he submitted this declaration, he had successfully participated in eight election  cycles under the ballot receipt deadline.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Ms. Notz, you  -- you keep going back --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: Yeah.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: -- to the facts of this case and I appreciate -- appreciate why.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: Mm-hmm.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: I would too. But I think what the Chief Justice is getting at and what would help me, certainly, is, okay, if a probability of -- of loss needs to be shown to secure standing, what's that probability?  Is it 50 percent?  Is it 60 percent?  You've resisted giving us a number, and I -- I -- I would just ask you if you could what you think that threshold should be. And then, along the way, is there something unseemly about federal courts making prognostications about a candidate's chance of success immediately before an election that itself might influence the election?  Thoughts?

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: Yes. So -- so I -- I -- I hear maybe two -- two questions in there. And I am resisting giving a number because that is consistent with this Court's cases. The Court has said --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Okay. So no number. You're not going to give us a number. How about the second part of the question?

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: Sure. And  --and maybe could you repeat that for one to --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Yeah. Is there something unseemly about a federal court in the middle of an election saying you don't have standing because you're going to win or you do have standing because you're going  -- you might lose and that that itself might influence the electoral process?

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: So, again, I don't -- I -- I  -- I think it is common across all of the Court's cases -- we're just asking for the same election rule --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: And I'm talking about in this context. And I'm sorry to interrupt.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: Yeah.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: But, in the election context, is there something particularly potentially unseemly about that, or are you not concerned about that?

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: I don't think it's more unseemly than in other cases where a plaintiff seeks to  --to establish standing based on a substantial  --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: All right.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: -- risk of a future harm.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAGAN
text: I mean, Ms. Notz  --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Then I -- then I just want to run a couple of hypotheticals by you if I might before I let you go and I'll let you go quickly, I promise. But imagine a law like the one in Janus or Illinois Socialist Workers where a state requires, you know, a lot of signatures to get on the ballot, minor party candidate has no chance of winning. Standing, you think?

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: I mean, yes, because, I mean, that case as I hear it describes a direct regulation of the candidate. And this Court  has long distinguished, you know, decades of cases between --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: We've never looked to the probability of success in those kinds of  cases, have we?

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: No, no, the Court has not. It's  --it's in cases like this one where the challenged law doesn't directly regulate the plaintiff, it regulates third parties. And in cases like these, the Court has held that the plaintiff needs to show a substantial risk of harm.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Okay, okay. So let's take an example that meets that, I think. Say the election officials decide to count only a hundred votes from each precinct and declare th e winner based on that, and assume the candidates don't know which side that random sample will benefit. Standing? Doesn't regulate them directly. It's just a rule about counting  ballots.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: So, as I understand the hypothetical, the election authority has announced in advance they're only going to count a small number of ballots. They're going to just disregard all the other ones?

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Yep.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: So I think actually, in Meese versus Keene, the Court, in addition to talking about loss of an election as a cognizable harm for candidates, also talked about damage to the candidate's reputation in the community. And I think the circumstance you're describing, like a pre -election announcement that we are just not going to count all the ballots, is the type of extreme circumstance where a candidate could say, if I win in that circumstance, my -- my victory is completely illegitimate.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Well, why?  Or -- or say  -- say -- say we're going to count ballots for three months after the election, and you don't know who  --who that's going to benefit. I can't prove that I'm going to win or lose. Or I'm going to count them for a year. Standing?

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: So I -- I -- so that -- I mean, that probably would kind of run  -- run into other Illinois laws and -- and federal laws that would --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Oh. Well, that's the allegation here, is that this runs into other laws, the practice here. And so I'm  giving you other examples, undercounting, overcounting, whatever -- however you want to phrase it, in which you don't know how it's  going to affect the candidate, but, you know, it  --one wonders.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: So I do think, in that type of circumstance, to me, that probably isn't the type of extreme circumstance where a candidate could claim, you know, reputational harm.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Okay. Thank you.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: What's reputation -- I mean --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: Yeah.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: -- you're referring to reputational harm. I'm trying to figure out, what's the reputational harm that distinguishes the sampling hypothetical that Justice Gorsuch asked from this case, where the allegation is that illegally cast ballots will be counted?  How is that different?

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: So  --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: That's the allegation.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: So, to me, there's a  --a distinction and -- between a situation where a candidate could perhaps plausibly allege that  even if he were elected, you know, under this process, the election would be so illegitimate that nobody would credit him as the successful candidate. And I don't think this circumstance meets that standard because, of course, Candidate Bost has successfully run for election now 10 times under the ballot receipt deadline, and I don't understand him ever to have suggested that he somehow was illegitimately elected. And the reputational harm component I do think comes from Meese versus Keene, which is a candidate standing case in which the Court described, you know, two types of injuries a candidate could have, and one was the risk of an election loss and the other was the possibility of, you know, adverse impact on their reputation in the community.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: I mean, I  --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAGAN
text: Suppose that  --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: Oh, go ahead. I don't want to create a bespoke standing rule. However, this case involves the  question of injury in a particular context which is different from other contexts, and  that is injury in a competition. So, along those lines, let me give you a hypothetical. Suppose that eight runners qualify for the U.S. finals to go to the Olympics in the hundred-meter dash, and when they show up for the competition, they find that actually they're going to have to run 105 meters. Does anybody have -- does -- does -- do any -- can any of them show injury in fact?

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: So I think, in that circumstance, you know, if this Court were, you know, to apply the competitive standing cases, the Court would, you know, ask was, you know, any  -- any potential plaintiff, as compared to a direct competitor, were they substantially disadvantaged by that?  And so, yes, they w ould need to show some sort of harm.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: So they would have to  -- an individual runner would have to show videotapes of other races and show I  -- I --I start to lose steam at the -- you know, the  97th meter, so making me go 105 yards is going to hurt me in relation to others?

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: I mean, I think the standard is one of plausibility. And I don't  know that one would need to present that type of evidence to make  --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: Well, then what --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: -- the assertion plausible.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: -- then what -- are any of them going to be able to challenge this?

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: I  -- I think, actually, it probably could be fairly easy to challenge if they could --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: How?

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: They could say  --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: How would they challenge?

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: I mean, presumably, I could imagine a plausible assertion that, you know, I have, you know, trained for a hundred-meter race and a 105 -meter race makes some sort of difference that puts me at a substantial disadvantage. But I guess I -- I -- you know, and I know the Court is resisting going back to the declaration, but standing cases are fact-specific.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: Well, this is -- in this specific situation, what would be wrong  with a rule that says four competitors in a competition where there's going to be a winner and there's going to be one or more losers, when the rules of competition are changed in a way that produces a risk that can't readily be measured, then all the competitors have standing?

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: So  --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: Doesn't that  -- doesn't that make sense?

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: So I don't think that it makes sense to adopt a blanket standing rule for candidates because I think it would create two problems. First, it would create chaos for election officials. It is very easy to be a candidate. Any self-declared candidate could challenge any election rule that they  happen to have a policy disagreement with, even if that rule were entirely harmless. And election s who are tasked with actually running elections would have to divert their time and  energy and litigate, you know, these policy -based disputes. And then federal courts, in turn, would be put in the position of  -- of resolving these, you know, disputes via advisory opinions, which is exactly what this Court's standing cases have dictated should not happen.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAGAN
text: So suppose that there was some change in rule that had a very high probability of cutting into a candidate's vote total by a fairly small amount, so let's say very high probability that this will cut into your vote total by 2 percent. Standing?

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: So I think, in that case, the candidate would have to be able to plausibly allege that that sort of 2 percent change in the margin harms him in some way. So  --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAGAN
text: Okay. So that seems -- that seems not right to me, that, you know, then you're going to force people to come into court and show a bunch of polls and how that 2 percent margin might or might not make a difference in the end when what you have is quite clear. What you have is a voting rule  that harms somebody relative to what's come before. And that is a usual standing inquiry. And, you know, it's not a bespoke anything. It's like this is a new rule. It's going to harm me relative to what's come before. I have a right to complain about it. Why isn't just that's enough?

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: I actually don't think we would have any problem at all with that rule. I think the problem is, is that Congressman Bost can't show standing based on that rule because then I would go back to the declaration  --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAGAN
text: I think he could show standing. Whether he did show standing is another thing entirely, right?  That this is a  -- is a complaint that sort of seems a little bit to be created in order to test a "I don't have to show injury at all" theory. But  -- but it would be very easy for Congressman Bost to write a complaint that satisfied my rule.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: I mean, I don't disagree with you and I, I guess, maybe appreciate you sort of re --- appropriately reframing. My point is that what he wrote at page 68 and 69  of his declaration does not satisfy that rule because, when asked about electoral loss, he  used the word "if."  He  --that  --that's a mere theoretical possibility of harm. He provides no explanation why he thinks he plausibly could lose his election. And when asked about a diminished margin of victory, he uses the word "may," which suffers from the same problem. He had a wealth of information available to him. I know I keep going back to the fact that he's an experienced candidate, but it matters. He had lived through, at the time he prepared this declaration, eight elections under the ballot receipt deadline. He said in his declaration:  I send poll watchers every single time. So he would have known at the end of the day on Election Day how many votes were cast on the unofficial --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAGAN
text: But what you're saying to me -- you know, I think that what you're saying to me is a little bit different than from what you said to the Chief Justice, because what you're  --because I agree with the Chief Justice. You do not want candidates to  have to walk into federal court and show that they're  -- you know, they're up in the polls by X amount or that they've won the last five elections by X amount. You're just saying he didn't say anything to show that he's going to be harmed at all by the new rule.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: That -- that's exactly our position. And, you know, the burden is on the plaintiff and -- and standing is fact-specific and you look at the record that the parties developed.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: You're walking away from a lot of your brief there.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: Yes, you are.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH

I guess I'm worried about the chaos of post-election litigation and how would that play out in a circumstance like a challenge to this particular ballot -counting rule. In particular, let's suppose post -election challenge; therefore, no real issue of standing in a real close election, and the rule is found invalid. Have you thought about what the  remedy would be in that circumstance?

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: So I -- I --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: And it presumably comes to this Court.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: Yeah.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Maybe the Hous e elections ride on it, so we know -- we know which way we rule what the impact will be, which is never a good position.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: So I guess I would push back on the idea that there  -- it necessarily would have to be resolved post -election. I'd go back to the point it's -- it's only substantial risk. There -- there is no need for certainty. He would simply, you know, have to show a substantial risk of some legally cognizable harm that could include losing the election. It could also, according to Meese,  you know, include, you know, harms that rise to the level of a reputational  --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: You --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: --harm. And I don't  -- I'm sorry. I just  --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Keep going. Sorry.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: I just wanted to point the Court's attention, as the Court is probably aware, to the Watson case out of the Fifth Circuit that challenges a very similar law. You know, in that case, the political party was found to have standing. It  --it did include, you know, different allegations, better allegations. So, for example, it included an allegation that if Mississippi's ballot receipt deadline was enforced, that would impair the party's ability to elect their Republican candidates. So I --I do think that it is -- standing is not hard to establish. I just think that this candidate did not establish it based on these  --the statements in the declaration.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: And the two things that  --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: Go ahead.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: The two things I think you've relied on are how close the election might be  -- you did say polling data earlier  -- and candidate -- expert candidates, and you've relied on how experienced the candidate is or how many terms. If a candidate's been elected twice, does that candidate have -- in a better position for standing?

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: So, I mean, I think that candidate -- I --I think the experience is relevant here just because Congressman Bost had so much personal knowledge about how the ballot receipt deadline works or doesn't work in his favor, about, you know, what these late-arriving ballots look like and whether they harm him or not. I think a newer candidate may not have that wealth of information, but they could certainly, I think, you know, rely on other information. Again, Meese talked about the experience of political advisors, of polling. I  -- I really -- I don't --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: Are you seriously arguing that whether or not the allegations here are sufficient requires an analysis of the particular background and experience of the  candidate who files the complaint?

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: No, not at  --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: This case would come out differently if this was somebody who had never run before?

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: My  -- my point is simply that Congressman Bost had a lot of information available to him that he could have used to explain. He could have said, for example, you know, I've been through eight election cycles under this deadline. This is a  --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: Well, then you are -- I mean, then you are referring to the particulars of his situation. In any event, let me talk  -- ask you about the pocketbook injury. Why isn't that straightforward? Mr. Clement says, look, it's -- it's political malpractice not to continue poll watching and  related activities until the -- the final bell actually tolls. That costs money. If you  extend the period, it costs me more money. That's a pocketbook injury. And your answer is, well, he didn't have to spend that, right?  That's your answer?

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: So, I mean, our answer is that when this Court has found standing basically based on a expenditure of resources -- that's, you know, his position -- the Court has required the plaintiff to demonstrate that that resource expenditure was undertaken to avoid a risk of harm that is itself legally cognizable. And I think that that rule makes good sense because, if I think -- if the rule were otherwise, the plaintiff could simply take a failed future injury theory of harm where they couldn't show a substantial risk of harm  --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: Wait.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: -- and --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: You think  -- you think the risk of losing the election is not legally cognizable?

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: Well, of course, Congressman Bost has not established a substantial risk he might lose an election. And, in fact, he told the Seventh Circuit  multiple times that he is not at risk of losing an election. I do think had he adequately established, you know, a substantial risk of losing an election, then, certainly, the pocketbook injury would be viable.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: So it turns on the risk of losing the election, not the risk of a  -- a less favorable result, less  -- a smaller margin?

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: I think it turns on a  -- a  -- a substantial risk of a legally cognizable harm, and I don't think that a diminished margin of victory in and of itself is a legally cognizable harm.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: But we're talking about injury in fact. Isn't a smaller margin of victory an injury in fact?

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: I don't think so because, unless it's coupled with something else, a smaller margin of victory has no real-world consequences.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: It has no real -world consequences?  Really?

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: I mean, unless a candidate could plausibly --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: It makes no difference if you win by 50.00000 percent versus 80 percent?  No, it doesn't matter, a win is a win?

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: I think, under those circumstances, a candidate probably could plausibly establish that a diminished margin of victory, you know, has a reputational or other competitive consequence that matters. But I don't think that under circumstances where the change in the margin is a vote or -- or a handful of votes, that that's a legally cognizable harm. And I think that's also consistent with the historical cases. I mean, if you look at the his torical circumstances under which a candidate could obtain an election recount, those were always circumstances where the recount was likely to change the outcome.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: The question Justice Alito started with was monetary injury. And I -- I thought that the likelihood of  winning the election was really irrelevant to that. You have to hire staff for an extra two weeks. And a good campaign is going to try to end up on Election Day with close to zero left in the bank to leave it all on the field. If you have to extend it two weeks, you're going to be reallocating your resources and potentially have to raise more money. But, at a minimum, you're going to have to spend more money, which is just obvious standing, isn't it, without getting into all this other stuff?  That's just obvious standing. You have to -- you have to spend more money to staff an extra two weeks.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: So  --so I  -- I don't think so. I think what this Court's cases stand for  -- and this is cases like Clapper and Alliance versus Hippocratic Medicine  --is the proposition that if a plaintiff is going to rely on the expenditure of resources to establish standing, the plaintiff needs to show that that expenditure was necessary to avoid a  substantial risk of an injury that is itself legally cognizable. And I think that that makes sense because I think that if the rule were otherwise, the r equirements for showing standing on a future injury theory would be watered down.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: I thought the --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: Can we just be  --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Oh, sorry.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: Oh, sorry.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Just one follow -up.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: Mm -hmm.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: I thought the test was is it part of your core activities, your ordinary activities, if the expenditure is part of that. And I would think, for a campaign, as  -- as the amicus brief, the ACLU, and the League of Women Voters was quoted before, and I had -- I had it too, political malpractice not to -- not to be ready for that, to staff that.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: So I think that  -- so --so Petitioners  here have not sort of proceeded under that organizational standing theory, but  I think, if you applied that theory here, we would still prevail because I think that  Congressman Bost's core mission is to win elections. He's -- he's never told us that  he has another -- I mean, maybe some other candidate would have some other core mission. A minor party candidate's core mission might be, you know, to bring attention to its message. But, because he's never --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Well --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: --proceeded under this theory --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: One more, sorry.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: Sure.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: But spending money to get out the vote, monitor the polls, have staff that does all that, which is going to be necessary for an additional two weeks is  --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: But just to be  --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: -- part of the campaign.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: I guess that -- that was my clarifying  --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Yeah.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: -- question because, with respect to this regulation, it's not the campaign that is extended for two weeks, is that correct?  I mean, I understood what is happening in this regulation is that it's just the counting of the votes that have been post- -- that come in postmarked, but the campaign is not continuing, right?

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: So, I mean, all this regulation means, and it doesn't even actually extend the time period for counting votes because we would be count -- the state would be counting provisional ballots during that 14 -day period regardless.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: So there's already counting going on. So the costs are really reduced. I mean, as I understand this regulation, what is happening is that the state has decided that it's going to count ballots that it receives in the mail that are postmarked as of Election Day for the next two weeks. So, really, what is the expenditure that is happening here?  I guess Mr. Bost is saying:  I have to have people to continue to  monitor the counting. But you say counting is happening anyway because of the provisional ballots. So I don't understand this great big cost that is suddenly happening.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: I mean, I -- I --I -- I mean, I don't mean to fight the question. That's probably a question for the Congressman. I mean, we did, you know, for purposes of this point in the proceeding, you know, take at his word that he has, you know, engaged, you know, additional resources to engage in further -- or in monitoring the counting. But I do agree with Your Honor's observation that the time period for the counting is not extended at all. And if I could, I see I'm short on time, but I'd like to, you know, briefly address, I think, Justice Kavanaugh, you know, raised the legal malpractice point, that sort of colorful phrase. I do think that Clapper is helpful on this point because, in Clapper, you know, there was no question that the lawyers there had diverted resources. They were traveling  overseas to meet with their clients and they were doing that because they wanted to avoid the risk of unlawful surveillance associated  with the challenged federal law. I don't think there was any question that those decisions were reasonable because there -- if you look at the Second Circuit's decision, there was an affidavit submitted by a legal ethicist, and the ethicist explained that if the lawyers didn't take precautions like these, they actually would be violating their duties as attorneys, essentially --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Thank you, counsel.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: -- committing --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Justice Thomas, anything further?  Justice Alito?

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: You think that monitoring the counting of paper ballots is either not important or doesn't require the expenditure of resources?

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: No. That's not our position. Of course, Congressman Bost is free to monitor countering -- you know, counting, you know, consistent with Illinois law. Our position is simply that when a plaintiff has -- seeks to establish standing  based on a resource-expenditure theory, the question isn't whether that decision was reasonable. The question isn't whether it was prudent. The question is whether -- were those resources expended to avoid a substantial risk of harm that is itself legally cognizable. And, as I mentioned, I think the rule makes sense because, if the rule were otherwise, a plaintiff could simply take a failed future-injury theory of standing where they couldn't show a substantial risk of harm and repackage it as a -- as a present-injury theory of standing based on resource expenditures.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: All right. Thank you.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Justice Sotomayor?  Justice Kagan? Justice Gorsuch? Justice Kavanaugh?

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Just one question. Justice Scalia once wrote  --and I know you're going to say that this case doesn't implicate this, but I just want to understand  if you agree with the principle that he said, which was:  "Count first and rule upon legality afterwards is not a recipe for producing election results that have the public acceptance democratic stability requires."  Do you agree with that?

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: I think  --theoretically, I think it -- it makes sense, you know, not to  -- if  --if I understood the statement, I -- I think that post-election challenges are probably not ideal. Did I understand the statement correctly?  But I don't think that our position, which, again, is how the Court treats standing across all cases, requires that because the test is simply substantial risk. And Congressman Bost's declaration simply doesn't show s ubstantial risk by any metric.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Thank you.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Justice Barrett?  Justice Jackson?

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: So I'm a little bit worried about your concession to Justice Kagan that the  --that you'd be okay with a rule that says that if the harm -- if it harms -- the challenged regulation harms someone relative to what had come before, that would be enough. And the reason I think is because that would implicate situations like even the one Justice Kagan posited, which is a person who has lost the election significantly but who claims something about the two -week period would change their margin, or -- lost or won, say, change their margin, would  --would be harmed by that. And I guess I don't understand that. It seems t o me that it might -- that the extra counting of ballots might change your position, but it only harms you if it would make a difference in the election. And I thought that was your bottom line. I thought it was sort of what the government was saying  -- the --the -- the SG was saying a little bit. But it seems to me crucial to uphold this idea that harm is required for standing purposes. And I worry a little bit practically if we accept that kind of thought, the idea  that a candidate is harmed if their margin of error changes even if it doesn't make a  difference in the election, that we're actually opening up avenues for a lot of post-election challenges that we wouldn't otherwise have, people who have lost the election but they want their margin of defeat to be different or they think it might have been, and so now we have litigation over the counting as a result of that. Can you --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: Yeah.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: -- respond?

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: So I appreciate the question. Thank you. I certainly did not mean to suggest, if I did, that a diminished margin of victory by itself in our view is a legally cognizable harm. So maybe it would kind of be, you know, helpful just to describe what we think our  legally cognizable harms for candidates, and I think they come from history, and I think they come from Meese versus Keene. The easy one is the risk, the substantial risk of losing an election. Then there are other concrete electoral consequences  that are probably more available to minority party candidates, but that would be like a substantial risk of not getting on the ballot, a substantial risk of not qualifying for public fund  --public fund -- public funding or maybe sort of other fund-raising injuries. And then there is the statement in Meese versus Keene which talks about reputational harms, and I think that in extreme circumstances, a candidate could plausibly allege in advance of an election that even if I win, I know I'm going to win, even if I win, under this election scheme, my victory will be so illegitimate that  --that my reputation will be harmed.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: And so, to summarize, those are the kinds of harms --

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: Exactly.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: -- that Justice Kagan says have been routinely alleged and  courts have accepted and are pretty easy to make, and so then you get on the -- the n you go on with your lawsuit, right?

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Jane E. Notz
text: Yes. Thank you.

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Thank you, counsel. Rebuttal, Mr. Clement?

case_name: Michael J. Bost, Et Al., Petitioners, V. Illinois State Board Of Elections, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Paul D. Clement
text: Thank you, Mr. Chief Justice. Just a few points in rebuttal. First, I just want to make the point that I don't think you should just contract all this out to the RNC and the DNC. There are cases where the RNC has lost on standing. On page  --page 16 of our petition, RNC against Burgess is one. But I also don't think you want to put the candidate in the position that they have to convince the national committee to support their challenge if they actually think they're being harmed either by the pocketbook or their electoral prospects or that unlawful ballots are going to be counted. Second, I think it's important when you look at this complaint -- and people are complaining about the threadbare nature of the complaint -- keep in mind one of the things that is in the complaint, and this is at 85a of the Petition Appendix, is the state's own statement before the previous election that  said, hey, reporters, don't get too excited about Election Day results because the late-arriving ballots can change the results, so stay tuned, essentially, for 14 days. Now the state didn't say, oh, but don't worry about Congressman Bost's district. That one's different. That's a state seat. And, of course, the state would never say that because that would put state election officials in a ridiculous position of, before the election, deciding that certain seats are safe seats and certain states  --seats are tossups. But yet the state wants to put the federal courts in the same position. They want you to look at this declaration and say, well, you know, he's a 10-time incumbent, so he's got a higher standard of showing how these ballots are going to hurt him. Or maybe it's easier for different -- for a different incumbent. That way lies madness, with all due respect. I mean, they're asking for  essentially an Article III determination that Congressman Bost is in a safe seat. And the Article III equivalent of the Cook Report seems like something that should be avoided at all costs. Now let me just finish on one point, which is part of the debate here is who's asking for a special rule of standing. And with respect, I think it's the state that's asking for a special rule of standing to the effect that only an electoral disadvantage that can threaten your win or loss at the end of the day counts and maybe some stuff that I'm, frankly, confused about about Meese and one or two things. But it's really like you got to  go in there and say this is going to be outcome-determinative in the election. That is a special rule for elections. They say pocketbook injuries don't count in this context. That  --that's not the law. I mean, if the government says to me, Clement, give me 500 bucks, that's a pocketbook injury. I don't have to point to some other injury that complements the pocketbook injury. Now there are certain cases where there's a very speculative primary injury, and then this Court has said, well, you can't spend yourself into standing. But that's not this case. It's perfectly reasonable to spend this  money on these -- poll watching. Political malpractice not to do it. Let me finish with one thought, is it seems like we have three different standard -- tests here, three different theories, but they all come down to a simple common-sense proposition. A candidate is not a bystander in his or her own election. Their name's on the ballot, they put their lives on hold, so they have a special interest in what's on the ballot. Thank you.
